title: Create Your Own Token
objectives: What mint authority is, and why its status decides everything
Why anyone can launch a token, and what that means when you buy one
That revoking mint authority fixes supply but doesn't make a project honest

steps.title: Anyone can mint a token
steps.body:
No permission needed. No application, no gatekeeper, no reviewer. You instruct the Solana Token program to create a <Term id="mint">mint</Term>, and you choose the name, the ticker, the decimals, and the starting <Term id="total_supply">total supply</Term>. The whole thing takes about thirty seconds and costs a few cents in fees and rent.

That is the feature. Permissionless means anyone can create an asset and a market for it, and no bank decides who gets to build.

Which is also why those same thirty seconds belong to scammers. Nobody audits a token before it launches, because there is no before. The token is live the moment the transaction lands. So the burden of checking what a token is allowed to do falls on the buyer, and there is no authority standing behind it. The rest of this lesson is about reading those settings.

steps.title: Mint authority: the printing press
steps.body:
When a mint is created it names a <Term id="mint_authority">mint authority</Term>: a single address that can create new tokens at any time, out of nothing.

Whoever holds that address holds the printing press. Every token they mint dilutes every existing holder, and they can sell the new supply into the market for free money. An active mint authority is one of the most common <Term id="rug_pull">rug pull</Term> setups in a new launch, precisely because it's invisible unless you look for it.

The honest move is to take it away. Revoking sets the mint authority to `None`, and because the Token program's code can't be changed, that's permanent: from that point the supply can never grow again. Not by the developer, not by anyone.

Hold onto one caveat, though. Revoking fixes the *maximum* supply. It does nothing about the tokens the creator already minted and kept - they can still sell those. Supply and distribution are two separate checks.

There's also a second switch on every mint, the freeze authority. If it's live, that address can freeze your token account and stop you transferring or selling. A launch that revoked mint authority but kept freeze authority has not actually given up control. That's the subject of B10.

steps.title: What is inside a mint account
steps.body:
A mint account is tiny - 82 bytes. That's the token's entire definition:

- `mint_authority`: an address, or `None`
- `supply`: the current total, as an integer
- `decimals`: how many places the integer scales by
- `is_initialized`: whether the account is set up
- `freeze_authority`: another address, or `None`

Revoking authority writes a `None` tag into those bytes. There's no admin panel and no override switch: the Token program will only mint when a valid authority signature is provided, and a `None` authority can never produce one.

So 'revoked' is a verifiable fact, not a founder's promise. Any block explorer shows you the same 82 bytes the program reads, and they either contain an address or they don't.

questions.prompt: What does revoking mint authority do to a token?
options: Destroys all tokens already in holders' wallets
Permanently fixes the maximum supply so no new tokens can ever be minted
questions.explainRight: The maximum supply is fixed for good. No signature can ever mint another token.
questions.explainWrong: It locks the supply permanently. After that, nobody can print more.

questions.prompt: If a memecoin creator keeps the mint authority active, what is the risk to buyers?
options: They can mint unlimited new tokens and sell them, diluting everyone
questions.explainRight: Unlimited minting. That is why an active mint authority is treated as a rug risk.
questions.explainWrong: Free printing. An active mint authority lets the creator create unlimited supply and sell it.
